newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN reports month-old massacre of 300 Burundi Hutus.
newsitem.headline: UN reports month-old massacre of 300 Burundi Hutus.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR on Friday reported a massacre of 300 Burundian Hutu refugees a month ago in Burundi's troubled northwestern Cibitoke region.
UNHCR spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume announced the killing of the refugees, who were on their way from Zaire, at a Geneva briefing.
Asked to explain why it took to announce the killing she said the UNHCR had just heard of the massacre and had no access to the area, the most dangerous in Burundi.
The Hutus were killed in a church in Murambi village in Cibitoke, where Hutu rebels and Burundi's almost exclusively Tutsi army are fighting a guerrilla war, she said.
They were among some 3,000 Burundian Hutus who fled a Tutsi revolt in east Zaire and crossed to Cibitoke.
UNHCR's special envoy to the region, Dessalegn Shefeke, was discussing the incident with the Burundi authorities, she added.
The latest massacre raises new questions over the forced return of Hutu refugees to their strife-ridden homelands where armies and governments are dominated by the Tutsi minority.

Some 35,000 Burundian Hutus have returned home from Zaire since the Tutsi rebellion there began a month ago. Another 500,000 Hutus from Rwanda have poured back into their country after Tutsi rebel shelling forced Hutu militiamen to flee.
The mass returns have pleased the UNHCR, which had tried unsuccessfully for two years to voluntarily repatriate them, as well as donors who paid $1 million a day to feed the refugees.
Before the latest crisis, U.S. and Western diplomats in the region privately advocated a forced but organised return.

Officials of the U.N. human rights office could not say immediately when they first heard of the Cibitoke massacre. They have only five observers in Burundi, mostly confined to Bujumbura because it is dangerous to travel to the countryside.
Western aid agencies pulled out of Cibitoke in June after three Swiss staff members of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) were killed in an ambush.
At least 150,000 people have died in the past three years in a civil war after Burundi's first elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup by Tutsi soldiers.
A senior U.N. human rights official said Burundian Hutu refugees should not be forced back into their homeland where they could face fresh attacks at the hands of the army.

"Our main concern is that these people fleeing Zaire are being sent to Cibitoke. These people should not be forced back to dangerous areas of Burundi," said Gomez Del Prado, U.N. human rights coordinator for field operations.
UNHCR announced the massacre a day after the London-based human rights group Amnesty International reported it.
Amnesty said it had documented killings, disappearances and ill-treatment occurring almost daily among the returnees with women, children, babies and the elderly among the victims.
